evidence.quote: The remains of the earth-lodge dwellings can be seen as large circular depressions in the ground.

evidence.claim: River bluffs, broad plains and bottomland forests meet at the Knife and Missouri rivers near Stanton.
evidence.quote: Scenic sights such as broad plains, river bluffs, and river bottom forests can all be seen along the two rivers.

evidence.claim: At the Washburn end of the journey, the Lewis and Clark Interpretive Center overlooks the Missouri and adjoins a rest stop serving Highways 83 and 200A.
evidence.quote: It is attached to a highway rest stop serving Highways 83 and 200A.

evidence.claim: At the Washburn end of the journey, the Lewis and Clark Interpretive Center overlooks the Missouri and adjoins a rest stop serving Highways 83 and 200A.
evidence.quote: overlooks the Missouri River on the outskirts of Washburn

evidence.claim: Travel here entered an established agricultural and trading landscape: Hidatsa and Mandan people traded corn alongside furs and other goods.
evidence.quote: Their trading largely consisted of furs, guns, and metals such as copper, but the Hidatsa and Mandan also traded corn and other agricultural products.

evidence.claim: The Lewis and Clark Expedition built Fort Mandan for the winter of 1804–1805.
evidence.quote: Fort Mandan was the name of the encampment which the Lewis and Clark Expedition built for wintering over in 1804–1805.

evidence.claim: When the party returned in August 1806, the fort had burned; later, the Missouri eroded its former site.
evidence.quote: the Missouri River has slowly eroded the bank and shifted course to the east, eroding away the former site of the fort.

evidence.claim: When the party returned in August 1806, the fort had burned; later, the Missouri eroded its former site.
evidence.quote: When the Corps passed back through the area in August 1806 on their return journey to the East, they found the fort had burnt to the ground.

evidence.claim: Start with the Knife River villages north of Stanton, then continue toward the Fort Clark site west of Washburn.
evidence.quote: The village is located ½ mile north of present-day Stanton

evidence.claim: Start with the Knife River villages north of Stanton, then continue toward the Fort Clark site west of Washburn.
evidence.quote: site located eight miles west of Washburn

evidence.claim: Near Washburn, Hensler lies beside railroad tracks close to Highway 200 Alternate.
evidence.quote: located along the BNSF railroad tracks near North Dakota Highway 200 Alternate

evidence.claim: Finish at the interpretive center and the separate Fort Mandan reconstruction, about two miles apart.
evidence.quote: It is located about two miles from the reconstructed Fort Mandan.

evidence.claim: Circular depressions mark earth lodges at the Knife River villages, where collapsed walls and roofs left visible rims.
evidence.quote: As the dwellings were abandoned, the walls and roof collapsed and created the visible outer circular rim.

evidence.claim: Some dwellings measured as much as 40 feet across.
evidence.quote: These dwellings were as large as 40 feet in diameter

evidence.claim: The villages formed a trading and agricultural center; women managed extensive gardens of corn, beans, squash and sunflowers.
evidence.quote: They raised corn, beans and squash as well as sunflowers in their extensive gardens which were managed by the women.

evidence.claim: Sakakawea, a Shoshone captive, lived in one of the Knife River villages.
evidence.quote: The Knife River Villages served as an important major central trading and agricultural area.

evidence.claim: Sakakawea, a Shoshone captive, lived in one of the Knife River villages.
evidence.quote: Sakakawea (Sacagawea) was a Shoshone captive who lived in one of the villages of the Knife River.

evidence.claim: The historic site preserves village remains, cache pits and traces of travois trails.
evidence.quote: there are the visible remains of earth-lodge dwellings, cache pits, and travois trails.

evidence.claim: Wooden lodge structures were covered with willows, dried grass and earth.
evidence.quote: They were made entirely of wood, covered by a layer of willows which was, in turn covered by a layer of dried grass.

evidence.claim: Wooden lodge structures were covered with willows, dried grass and earth.
evidence.quote: The grass layer was covered by about 4 inches of earth

evidence.claim: A central fireplace vented through a hole in the roof.
evidence.quote: The fireplace was in the center and a hole in the roof allowed the smoke to get out.

evidence.claim: Lodge depressions and an unmarked cemetery with more than 800 graves remain at Fort Clark.
evidence.quote: Lodge depressions are also visible along with an unmarked cemetery with more than 800 graves.

evidence.claim: Mandan people built an earth-lodge settlement on the Missouri bluffs in 1822.
evidence.quote: In 1822, the Mandan tribe built a settlement with earth-covered lodges on the bluffs of the Missouri River.

evidence.claim: James Kipp of the American Fur Company established a trading post south of the village in 1830.
evidence.quote: In 1830, a representative of the American Fur Company named James Kipp built Fort Clark Trading Post south of the village.

evidence.claim: In 1837, passengers infected with smallpox arrived aboard the St.
evidence.quote: In 1837, the steamboat St. Peters docked at the village carrying passengers infected with smallpox, and sparking the 1837 Great Plains smallpox epidemic. As the disease swept through the village, it wiped out approximately ninety percent of the inhabitants.

evidence.claim: Arikara people moved into the abandoned village in 1838.
evidence.quote: In 1838, the nearby Arikara tribe moved into the abandoned village.

evidence.claim: A second trading post followed in 1850.
evidence.quote: In 1850, another trading post was built by Charles Primeau. In 1851, a cholera outbreak occurred and then a smallpox outbreak in 1856. When an attack by the Dakota happened in 1861, the fort was permanently abandoned.

evidence.claim: The Fort Mandan near Washburn is a reconstruction of the expedition’s winter quarters.
evidence.quote: A replica of the fort has been constructed near the original site.

evidence.claim: The original was triangular, built from cottonwood cut along the riverbanks, with its gate facing the Missouri.
evidence.quote: The fort was built of cottonwood lumber cut from the riverbanks.  It was triangular in shape, with high walls on all sides, an interior open space between structures, and a gate facing the Missouri River

evidence.claim: Its precise location is uncertain and is believed to lie beneath the river.
evidence.quote: The precise location is not known for certain. It is believed now to be under the water of the river.

evidence.claim: The reconstruction follows materials and designs described in the expedition journals.
evidence.quote: Made according to materials and design as described in the expedition's journals

evidence.claim: Nearby, the interpretive center also addresses Mandan and Hidatsa farming cultures and the fur trade at Fort Clark.
evidence.quote: including the farming-based cultures of the Mandan and Hidatsa Native American nations, the fur trade at Fort Clark Trading Post State Historic Site

evidence.quote: bunks the men slept in
